toc.title: Stuck defense doesn't go away with age
The goal isn't to climb out right away

blocks.p: A listener asked me whether we can co-regulate with someone who traumatized us. Please put yourself first with this one. It might be challenging. You may relate, and you might have the same question about people in your own life, especially parents. The answer is more complex than you might think, so check in with yourself as you read.
These are my general thoughts, not specific advice to her or to you. I'll take her question in pieces.

blocks.h: Stuck defense doesn't go away with age

blocks.p: She wrote:

q: "I have a question about climbing up the ladder from a sympathetic state, particularly in family relationships. A source of childhood trauma for me was my dad. I started going on a journey of trauma healing through therapy and self-help in my 30s, but now, even as a 40-year-old adult, I still get into a state of defensive energy right away when my dad and I interact."

blocks.p: No matter our age, even at the old, old age of 40 (I was right there with her at the time, so I'm allowed to say that), we still get into these defensive states. Around a certain person, or in a certain environment, that defensive energy can come up. The sympathetic state doesn't just go away. It's there for a reason. We may have had to use it growing up, maybe got stuck in it, and that could be with a parent.

It doesn't go away with age, unfortunately. It really takes the work. It takes accessing and building the strength of our vagal brake. So even if sympathetic energy isn't a problem in other contexts, it could very well be a problem in certain ones, and that's super normal, especially around traumatic or potentially traumatic events. If that trauma hasn't been healed, if we haven't gotten unstuck from it, it's expected that the defensive energy will come right back in that context. So throw away the age, and let's look at this as stuck defensive energy.

It could be freeze trauma: stuck frozen energy, where we're mobilized and shut down at the same time, and that freeze shock trauma can resurface in certain situations. Or it could be that we had to live in a state of defense, whether flight, fight, or shutdown, and when we're back in those contexts, it comes up again.
A helpful, and I think necessary, first step for anyone is to normalize and validate your feelings and your polyvagal state.

To normalize means to look at the context of what you went through, what childhood was like, and then at how you feel now: your state, your feelings, even the stories in your mind. And then say, "This is what I went through, and this is where I'm at right now. Yeah, that makes sense. That's what I would expect."

To validate means you're recognizing the feelings that are there and allowing them to be there. If a friend told me how they felt and I said, "Yeah, it sounds like you're feeling that," they would feel validated. Their feelings would be seen and understood. Not judged, not minimized. "Yes, I see that feeling in you," and that's it. We can do that for ourselves too: "This is how I feel. I do feel this way around this person." No minimizing, no judging. It is what it is.
I know that when we're in a sympathetic state, we want answers: solutions, coping skills, grounding skills. What to do about it can come next. First, normalize and validate.
She went on:

q: "I go into sympathetic, and I immediately want to flee and make distance between us. Otherwise, I will go further down the ladder into fight mode, and I can sense that my voice, language, and body just feel more activated and aggressive. It's awkward because he's visiting me and staying in my home for now. I'm trying to climb out of sympathetic in these moments, but my vagal brake isn't as strong when it comes to interacting with my dad. There is a lot of trauma history in our relationship, and I feel so disconnected from him."

blocks.p: I never want to minimize anybody's upbringing. But the way I would treat this as a therapist, or what I'd say to a friend, changes with the history.

If we're living with someone who sexually abused us growing up, and he hasn't made any change and is still a dangerous person in some fashion, that is a hell of a lot different from a parent who wasn't capable of building a healthy attachment because of their own stuff. And that second one describes pretty much any parent, period.

The parent who loved you but didn't know how to show it and was very distant. Or loved you and didn't know how to connect with you. Or loved you and was very judgmental. We can call that trauma. We can call it a lack of healthy attachment, or a severed relationship. But the flavor of it, and the hope of improvement, is a hell of a lot more than with the person who was abusive and has never recognized it, never made amends, never apologized, never gotten treatment or done their own work.

The parent who did their best and just wasn't capable of a healthy attachment, which maybe left that child more in a shutdown state: as a therapist, I feel like I could work with that parent pretty easily. They want to, but they don't know how. I've talked with so many parents who fit that bill, and when we can get a dialogue going, change can happen really fast. The parent in denial is a hell of a lot more difficult to work with. If a friend told me about that really abusive flavor, I wouldn't say, "Just talk it out and give him a hug and everything's okay."

And if things are still not safe, if there's still abuse going on in whatever form, that changes everything about how we look at this, whether as a therapist, a friend, or a podcast host hearing the situation.

So it's messy. I don't think there's a clear answer, and the answer isn't the first step anyway. It will be different based on the context, the people, a lot of factors. I think if you're in a situation like this, you'll know the answer once you're well regulated enough, and I don't think you can predict what it will be. Once you're in a state of safety, with healthy boundaries, listening to your values, expecting a certain standard of behavior from others, the way you look at the situation is significantly different. The answers you come up with, your creativity, all of it changes.

Even as a therapist, I don't give answers. I don't think it's my job, or appropriate, to tell people what to do. I never recommend that my clients cut family out of their lives. If that's a solution they come to on their own, fine. Healthy boundaries, though? Hell yeah. Healthy boundaries are always a good idea.

blocks.h: The goal isn't to climb out right away

blocks.p: What's more appropriate here is more validation. She wrote, "I'm trying to climb out of sympathetic in these moments." I get it, and good job. But also, not good job. We can all relate to this.

Being in sympathetic doesn't mean something is wrong. It feels bad, but those feelings might be very accurate. I don't know the context, but based on history, and maybe even on the present context, those feelings may be dead-on accurate. Trying to climb out of sympathetic when it's needed wouldn't make a lot of sense.

And more generally, just because we're in a state doesn't mean the goal is to get out of it. The goal is to be with the state and attune to it. Now, if you're in a situation that's actually dangerous, we don't want to mindfully close our eyes and be with the energy. We want to get the hell out of the situation. But in general, we want to feel these feelings outside of the dangerous context, on their own, when we have safety to balance them out.

So don't wait for the moment you're with that person and already feeling the defensive energy. Tap into it outside of that situation, when you're safe, when your safety anchors are available, in a safe environment or with safe people. You want to be able to self-regulate while feeling the defensive energy.
Here's generally how I think this works:

ol: Go to your safe spot. When that person isn't around, go to the place where you feel safe. Have whatever you think you'll need with you: movement, sensory things, a memory.
Validate and normalize. Acknowledge how you feel, and let it make sense.
Let it come up. Let the sympathetic energy come back up. That's okay. It's not a bad thing. Feel it just a bit, or as much as you can handle. Don't push it too far.
Use your safety anchor. Come back to safety.

blocks.p: That's how we discharge sympathetic energy: we tap into these feelings outside the context, in a place of safety, and let ourselves feel them. You can journal around it. You can meditate around it. You can draw, or dance it out, whatever creative outlet you have. If meditating into it and letting that discharge happen is something you can do, have at it. It's not for everybody, and it's not easy. If you want to feel the sympathetic energy and then do something that discharges it, like strangling a paper towel roll, or pushing against a wall and really feeling it in your muscles, that might be a good idea.

But you feel it while you're safe. In the moment itself, it could be crisis mode. I don't want to say too late, but it's a hell of a lot harder to self-regulate when you're in a moment that might require some danger energy.

blocks.p: She continued:

q: "We do have some brief moments of connection, but there are enough moments of sympathetic activation that keep us distant. To be honest, I'm hesitant to make the first steps to repair things between us. It just feels so weird, awkward, and even scary. I get a tingly sensation in my chest and a knot in my gut because of past trauma. Misunderstandings between us are left unresolved. I don't feel comfortable being the first one to reach out and repair."

blocks.p: Those are the feelings we have whenever we go outside our comfort zone. Trying to mend a relationship can be awkward, scary, and definitely weird.

Ideally, and I think the word "should" applies here, it should be the parent who reaches out first, even with adult children: "I messed up. I messed up really bad. I'm sorry. I want to mend things. I respect that you might not want to. I'm here if you change your mind. I'm doing my own work. I'm going to therapy once a week." Whatever that sounds like.

Realistically, that often won't happen. For some generations, that's just not okay. For my generation, I think those are conversations we can have with our kids, and I hope I'm modeling that for mine. But in situations like this, the parent might never be the one to step up and say, "We need to work on this. I'm working on myself."

At the same time, it's okay to let yourself feel those moments of connection, if they're true. If you're both feeling awkward and smiling through it, that's still something. But if nothing has changed, if the other person is still in deep denial, doesn't take you seriously, doesn't want to change, and you're smiling through that, that doesn't seem genuine to me.
So discern: is this a genuine moment of connection? Is there empathy happening, eye contact, smiling, maybe eye squints? Do they understand how I feel? Do I feel understood? If so, soak it up.

It's also okay to comment on those moments and say you appreciate them. You don't want to make it awkward. You don't want to say, "Why don't we do this more often?" or "Why couldn't you have done this 20 years ago?" But you can say, "I really appreciated this moment with you. Thank you. I love you." Bring some conscious awareness to it: "This meant something to me."

At the same time, you don't want to get your hopes up, and this is pretty common. We want our parent, or our spouse, or whoever, to follow through next time, so we feel understood all over again. That might not happen, depending on where they are in their own change process. So appreciate the moment, and with healthy boundaries and your values first, be realistic about whether it will happen again. Keep both in mind. And if these people are still unsafe in some way, we have to prioritize that.
Her last paragraph:

q: "Deep down, I want for my dad and I to be able to co-regulate and have a relaxed and attuned relationship. But because of my childhood trauma, I wonder if it is even practical for me to try to create a co-regulating relationship. Can co-regulation happen if the one person making the repair is a traumatized individual who has been traumatized by the other? It's been a challenge for me to climb up the ladder from a sympathetic state in those activated moments when I'm engaged with my dad. I'm wondering, during arguments or misunderstandings when we're in flight-fight mode, if there are some techniques or behaviors to help us repair and co-regulate to somehow get us both into a safe and social state."

blocks.p: Are there techniques and behaviors? Probably, and I don't know what they'd be for anyone in particular. You'd have to be curious about that on your own. But that's part of the problem: when two people aren't co-regulating and there's a history of trauma, do both of them even want to work on it together? I think both people have to have some investment in making things better. There are ways to cope and ground yourselves in these situations, but you both have to want to use them, and probably talk about that beforehand and come at it together.

Can we provide co-regulation without the other person being willing to accept it? Yes and no. We can still offer our cues of safety. But co-regulation isn't something we consciously do. We can consciously feel our stuck energy and self-regulate. That's different from co-regulation.

Co-regulation happens after one person is sufficiently self-regulated. That person gives off natural cues of safety without having to think about it. They naturally have more vocal prosody, more eye crinkles. They naturally smile when appropriate. And as that person, that mammal, gives off cues of safety, the other one picks up on them.

That doesn't mean the other person will change their behavior, or be able to climb their own ladder, or have any familiarity with how to feel safe. It depends so much on who's in the room, the context, the history of the traumatic stuff, and especially that person's motivation to change and how much awareness they have of their own state and feelings.

You can't force someone to regulate. Co-regulation isn't exactly a tool, because a tool is something we choose to use with some conscious direction. Co-regulation is the spontaneous showing of safety that happens naturally when we're in our ventral vagal state of safety and social engagement. We don't say, "Okay, now I'm going to smile, throw this cue of safety at someone, and watch their behavior change." That's not how it works. And even if you could smile or crinkle your eyes on purpose, the rest of your body can't fake it. If you're smiling but you're not really in your safety state, people pick up on that disingenuous smile, because the rest of the body might be tense. It won't come across as natural or genuine.

Is it practical to try to create a co-regulating relationship? To me, it depends so much on the other person's willingness to make change. If someone is fed up with their own state and trying to work their way up their own polyvagal ladder, they're much more likely to accept someone's co-regulation. They know something better is out there. If the person in your life just isn't ready for change, they can still pick up on your cues of safety, but what's their capacity to make actual change? I don't know.

Can co-regulation happen if the person making the repair was traumatized by the other? Technically, yes. Can the traumatized person, later in life, develop their vagal brake enough to offer cues of safety even around the person who harmed them? I think so. Do they have to? No. This is not a prescription. Is it likely? I don't know. I think it would take a lot of work: really strong, healthy boundaries and a very strong sense of self, to be back in that context around that person and still access your state of safety and social engagement. That's a tall order.

Keeping it under control doesn't mean you're in your safe and social state. Being around that person and gritting your teeth and bearing it just means you're keeping it together. That's great, and it has its usefulness. But it's a hell of a lot different from being in your ventral vagal state of safety and social engagement and genuinely feeling safe. So can we be around people who are genuinely triggering for us and keep it together enough to get through? Yes. But that's not co-regulation.

Co-regulation comes after one person is self-regulated. That's essential to the process. In a situation like this one, I don't hear that either person is sufficiently self-regulated to offer co-regulation, and in the context she describes, that's a tall order.

Co-regulation won't happen without genuine feelings of safety in one or both people. And even if one person gets there, the other can pick up on it, but it might be really uncomfortable for them, because they're not used to feeling safe and connected and getting those cues of safety. It might be really difficult for them to accept it, to be with that discomfort and vulnerability, and then to maintain it. It's a lot.

Those are my thoughts. I don't know the answer, and even if I did, I wouldn't want to give it to you, because I feel like that's inappropriate. I hope they bring some clarity if you're in a situation like this, and get you thinking about who you try to co-regulate with.
